summary: Describes four existing implementations of SPIRITS-like services, which start in the telephone network and need interaction with Internet services.

eli5.summary: Some phone events can trigger Internet actions. This describes four early ways companies built that.

questions: how do pstn and internet systems work together
subtitle: Four early ways to notify Internet users of incoming phone calls

tldr.problem: When someone is using their phone line for Internet access, incoming calls are lost or interrupt the connection. Phone companies and users need a way to handle these calls.
tldr.mechanism: Four implementations (Korea Telecom, Lucent, NEC, and Telia/Nortel) created systems that notify users of incoming calls over the Internet and let them choose how to handle each call without losing their Internet connection.
tldr.outcome: These prototypes proved the concept of Internet Call Waiting was feasible. All four implementations used Intelligent Network technology on the telephone side and SIP or proprietary protocols for Internet communication, providing a blueprint for the SPIRITS standard.

today: RFC 2995 is an Informational RFC that was published in November 2000 to document the state of early PSTN-Internet integration before standards were finalized. It has not been updated or obsoleted. The implementations described here served as proof-of-concept for the SPIRITS and PINT frameworks.

sections.title: Internet Call Waiting Service
sections.content:
This document describes four existing implementations of Internet Call Waiting (ICW), a service that lets people using their phone line for Internet access receive notifications of incoming calls. When a call arrives, the subscriber is notified via a pop-up window on the PC without interrupting the modem connection. The subscriber can then choose to accept the call (which terminates the Internet connection), reject it, forward it to another number, send it to voicemail, or set up automatic call handling based on pre-defined rules.

All four implementations studied here (Korea Telecom, Lucent Technologies, NEC, and Telia in cooperation with Nortel Networks) support ICW, which is the benchmark service for PSTN-initiated Internet services. This was a significant achievement because each implementation had to bridge two entirely different network architectures: the traditional telephone system and the Internet.
sections.eli5: When your phone line is busy with the Internet, this service catches incoming calls and tells your computer about them. You then pick what happens to the call without having to hang up from the Internet.

sections.title: Shared Architecture Patterns
sections.content:
All four implementations follow a similar pattern: they combine Intelligent Network (IN) technology on the PSTN side with new server systems on the Internet side. The PSTN part (Service Control Point, Service Switching Point, and Intelligent Peripheral) detects when the called party is busy on the Internet and triggers the ICW service. The Internet part includes a central server that manages ICW clients running on subscriber PCs and acts as a gateway between the two networks.

Three of the four implementations use the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) for communication between the PSTN and Internet. NEC's implementation is the exception, using a proprietary protocol, though NEC planned to add SIP support. All implementations use IN-based solutions for the PSTN side, demonstrating consensus on that part of the architecture.
sections.eli5: The phone network detects you are busy on the Internet and sends a message to an Internet server. That server tells your PC about the call, and after you choose what to do, it tells the phone network how to handle the call.

sections.title: Call Handling and Features
sections.content:
When a call arrives at a busy line, the subscriber is presented with a pop-up dialog showing the calling party's number and name (if available) and the time of the call. The subscriber can then choose from several options: accept the call over the PSTN (terminating the Internet connection), accept the call over the Internet using VoIP (if supported), reject the call, play a pre-recorded message, forward to voicemail, or forward to another number.

All four implementations support some form of automatic call handling. Subscribers can set up profiles with pre-defined dispositions for calls from specific numbers or define a default behavior when they do not respond within a set time. Some implementations also provide a detailed log of all incoming calls, including the caller information, the chosen action, and whether that action was successful.
sections.eli5: Your computer shows you who is calling. You pick what happens: answer the call (and lose the Internet), answer it by voice over the Internet (if your setup supports it), reject it, or send it somewhere else like voicemail.

sections.title: Protocol Choices
sections.content:
Korea Telecom's implementation uses PINT (PSTN/Internet Interworking Protocol) Version 1.0, which is based on SIP 2.0 with extensions for telephone services. The implementation employs PINT's REGISTER, INVITE, ACK, BYE, and CANCEL methods to manage the registration of ICW clients, notification of incoming calls, confirmation of call disposition, and termination of service sessions.

Lucent's implementation also uses SIP, with encrypted messages exchanged with the PC client and plain-text SIP over a secure intranet with the PSTN infrastructure. NEC uses a proprietary protocol based on remote operations over UDP/IP for the SPIRITS client-server interface, with plans to migrate to SIP. Telia/Nortel chose to run services on top of SIP Redirect Servers, allowing services to be developed and deployed across both PSTN and Internet networks using SIP as the common language.
sections.eli5: Different companies chose different ways to send messages between the phone network and the Internet. Three picked SIP (an Internet calling protocol). NEC used its own method but planned to switch to SIP later. Telia/Nortel used SIP redirect servers to treat all networks as if they were the same.

sections.title: Interoperability Challenges
sections.content:
The document explicitly states that not all pre-SPIRITS implementations inter-operate with each other. The implementations use different versions of SIP and different approaches to gateway and server architecture, which prevents seamless operation between them. This lack of interoperability was one of the key motivations for the SPIRITS Working Group to develop standardized inter-networking interfaces for PSTN-Internet services.

Despite these differences, the survey provides valuable insights. The convergence on IN-based PSTN solutions shows consensus on how to handle the telephone network side. The predominance of SIP use demonstrates recognition of SIP's strengths for this application, even among vendors who did not yet fully adopt it. These lessons informed the development of standards that would allow future implementations to work together reliably.
sections.eli5: The four systems could not talk to each other because they used different protocols and designs. This was a big reason why people worked on making a standard way to do it so future systems could work together.
